white.name: London vs ...Nf6 and ...e6
white.moves: d4 d5 Bf4 Nf6 e3 e6 Nf3 Bd6 Bg3 O-O Nbd2 c5 c3 Nc6 Bd3
white.idea: Build the same pyramid every game: pawns on c3, d4, e3, bishop out BEFORE e3, knights on f3 and d2. You win games here by knowing the plan, not by memorising lines.

notes.3: The bishop comes out first, before the e-pawn locks it in. That is the whole point of the London.
notes.5: Now e3 is safe: the bishop already has its diagonal.
notes.9: Bg3 offers the trade on d6 and keeps the bishop alive. If they take, recapture with the h-pawn and you have a free open h-file.
notes.11: Nbd2, not Nc3. The c-pawn wants c3 to hold d4.
notes.15: Bd3 aims at the kingside. Castle next, then think about Ne5 and f4.

white.name: London vs ...c5
white.moves: d4 d5 Bf4 c5 e3 Nc6 c3 Nf6 Nd2 e6 Ngf3 Bd6 Bg3 O-O Bd3
white.idea: Against the ...c5 break, keep c3 and the pawn chain. If they take on d4, recapture with the e-pawn and keep the centre.

notes.5: e3 now. If ...cxd4, exd4 is fine: you have an open e-file and a solid centre.
notes.7: c3 stops ...Nb4 and ...Qb6 raids. Solid, if a little dull. Dull wins at blitz.
notes.9: Nd2 supports e4 later and leaves c3 free for the pawn.

white.name: London vs the King's Indian set-up
white.moves: d4 Nf6 Bf4 g6 Nf3 Bg7 e3 O-O h3 d6 Be2 Nbd7 O-O
white.idea: Against ...g6, play h3 to keep your bishop from being kicked, then castle and aim for c3 and Nbd2. A quiet start; the pawn break e4 comes later.

notes.9: h3 gives your bishop a retreat square on h2. Play it before ...Nh5.
notes.11: Be2, not Bd3, if they threaten ...c5 and ...Nh5. Keep it flexible.

white.vs: Black plays the Modern or King's Indian: ...g6, ...Bg7

white.name: Chigorin: 2.Nc3 and Bf4
white.moves: d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 e6 e3 Bd6 Bg3 O-O Bd3 c5 Nf3
white.idea: Your most-played opening: 108 games, about 62%. Knight to c3 first, then the bishop. You leave the c-pawn free to push to c4 when it suits.

notes.3: Your Chigorin move. It stops ...e5 ideas and fights for e4 and d5 at once.
notes.5: The bishop comes out before e3. Same rule as the London.
notes.9: The bishop trade offer again. Always recapture towards the centre.

white.name: Accelerated London: early Bf4
white.moves: d4 Nf6 Bf4 e6 e3 c5 c3 Nc6 Nd2 d5 Ngf3 Bd6 Bg3 O-O Bd3
white.idea: Whatever move order they choose, the same setup works. You have scored about 67% with the accelerated London. Trust it.

white.name: Englund Gambit: take the pawn, keep calm
white.moves: d4 e5 dxe5 Nc6 Nf3 Qe7 Bf4 Qb4+ Bd2 Qxb2 Bc3 Bb4 Qd2 Bxc3 Qxc3 Qxc3+ Nxc3
white.idea: You have met the Englund 45 times (53%). Take the pawn, develop, and when they grab b2 with the queen, trap it: Bc3 and Qd2 and the queen is nearly lost.

notes.3: Take it. It is an unsound gambit; your job is to be sensible.
notes.5: Bf4 is a clean developing move. Nf3 and Bf4 and you are comfortable.
notes.9: Bc3 attacks the rook on a1 and the queen on b2 has no escape squares except by trading.

black.name: Caro-Kann: Advance
black.moves: e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nf3 e6 Be2 c5 Be3 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6
black.idea: Your light-squared bishop is out BEFORE the pawn chain locks it in. The e5 pawn is a target: attack the base (d4) with ...c5.

notes.6: Bf5 first. The classic Caro idea.
notes.11: ...cxd4 hits the centre. White's e5 pawn is overextended.

black.name: Caro-Kann: Classical
black.moves: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5 Ng3 Bg6 h4 h6 Nf3 Nd7 h5 Bh7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 Bf4 Ngf6 O-O-O Be7
black.idea: The standard Caro position. Your pawns are healthy and the bishop is safe on h7 (or trades off). No weak pawns, no early disasters.

notes.7: ...h6 gives the bishop a retreat square. Without it, h4-h5 traps it.
notes.14: Trade the good bishop. You have a solid game with no weaknesses.

black.name: Caro-Kann: Exchange
black.moves: e4 c6 d4 d5 exd5 cxd5 c4 Nf6 Nc3 e6 Nf3 Be7 cxd5 Nxd5 Bd3 Nc6 O-O O-O
black.idea: White is the one with the isolated queen's pawn after the dust settles. Blockade it with a knight on d5 and trade pieces.
black.vs: White exchanges on d5, then plays c4

black.name: Caro-Kann: 2.Nc3 and ...Bg4
black.moves: e4 c6 Nc3 d5 Nf3 Bg4 h3 Bxf3 Qxf3 e6 d4 Nf6 Bd3 Nbd7
black.idea: Against the quieter 2.Nc3, trade your bishop for the knight on f3 if they let you, then build with ...e6 and ...Nf6.

black.name: Slav Defence
black.moves: d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4 Bf5 e3 e6 Bxc4 Bb4 O-O Nbd7
black.idea: You win the pawn on c4 and hold it with ...Bf5 and ...Bb4 (or ...b5 if safe). The ...c6 structure is solid: your bishop is outside the pawn chain.

notes.8: Take on c4, then play a4 yourself? No: White's a4 stops ...b5. Plan: ...Bf5, ...e6, ...Bb4.
notes.10: The bishop comes out BEFORE ...e6. The same rule as the Caro.

black.name: Exchange Slav
black.moves: d4 d5 c4 c6 cxd5 cxd5 Nc3 Nf6 Bf4 Nc6 e3 Bf5 Nf3 e6
black.idea: Symmetrical and drawish on paper, but your pieces are comfortable and White has nothing special. A good way to meet a player who wants simplicity.

black.name: Versus the London System
black.moves: d4 d5 Bf4 c5 e3 Nc6 c3 Qb6 Qb3 c4 Qxb6 axb6 Nd2 e6 Ngf3 Bd6
black.idea: Strike the London early: ...c5, ...Qb6. If they offer the queen trade you get a healthy structure and the half-open a-file.

notes.4: The point: the b2 pawn is attacked. White must respond.
notes.9: The queens come off. You get the a-file and a decent pawn structure.

black.name: Versus the Réti and 1.Nf3
black.moves: Nf3 d5 g3 Nf6 Bg2 e6 O-O Be7 d3 O-O Nbd2 c5 e4 Nc6
black.idea: Take the centre with ...d5 and ...c5 and let White come to you. Easy to play, easy to understand.

lessons.title: The Opera Game
lessons.src: Morphy vs the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard, Paris, 1858
lessons.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 Bg4 dxe5 Bxf3 Qxf3 dxe5 Bc4 Nf6 Qb3 Qe7 Nc3 c6 Bg5 b5 Nxb5 cxb5 Bxb5+ Nbd7 O-O-O Rd8 Rxd7 Rxd7 Rd1 Qe6 Bxd7+ Nxd7 Qb8+ Nxb8 Rd8#

notes.7: Morphy takes the centre pawn and gets his pieces out. Development beats material.
notes.13: Qb3 hits both f7 and b7. A double attack on move 7.
notes.21: A sacrifice to keep the attack alive: knight takes b5 to pull open the b-file and the d-file.
notes.25: The plan: every piece in the attack, all of them at once.
notes.33: Queen sacrifice, forced mate. Notice that every move comes with a threat.

lessons.title: Evans Gambit: the attacking set-up
lessons.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 b4 Bxb4 c3 Ba5 d4 exd4 O-O d6 cxd4 Bb6 Nc3 Na5 Bg5 f6 Bf4

notes.7: A pawn sacrificed on move 4 to win time. Open files and a big centre are worth more than a pawn.
notes.11: d4 forces the issue before Black is developed.
notes.13: Castle, then recapture. Never rush: White gets the centre back with interest.
notes.17: Knight to c3 adds a fourth attacker to the centre and the e-file.

lessons.title: Najdorf: Kasparov's main structure
lessons.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5 Nb3 Be6 f3 Be7 Qd2 O-O O-O-O Nbd7 g4

notes.2: Fight for d4 at once. The Sicilian trades a wing pawn for a centre pawn.
notes.10: ...a6 stops Nb5 and prepares ...b5. The Najdorf's trademark waiting move.
notes.12: ...e5 hits d4 and gives Black a strong central grip, at the price of a hole on d5.
notes.19: White castles long and storms with g4. Black counterattacks on the c-file. This is the sharpest mainline in chess.

lessons.title: The London plan (typical Carlsen set-up)
lessons.src: A model sequence; Carlsen's London games follow this shape (not a single game)
lessons.moves: d4 d5 Bf4 Nf6 e3 c5 c3 Nc6 Nd2 e6 Ngf3 Bd6 Bg3 O-O Bd3 b6 Ne5 Bb7 f4

notes.3: Solid, boring, and in good hands very hard to beat. Carlsen has used it as a weapon to get a long game.
notes.11: Both knights develop first, pointing at e5.
notes.17: Ne5 is the key outpost. Support it with f4 and the kingside is yours.
